newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Competition leaves Bezeq outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Competition leaves Bezeq outlook cloudy.

text.p: Bezeq Israel Telecom has started facing the chill winds of competition in its key international calling business but analysts say they are not sure just how strong the firm will be.
"We don't have any experience in competitive markets. It's very difficult to gauge customer loyalty and price sensitivity," said Boaz Levitan, an analyst at Sahar Securites in Tel Aviv.
Israel's international calling market was thrown open to competition this month as the government authorised two concerns to begin offering services alongside state-owned Bezeq.

The new competition comes just as the Israeli government announced an agreement on Monday for Merrill Lynch to take a 12.5 percent equity holding in Bezeq for sale to Merrill Lynch clients. The deal is worth $250 million.
Bezeq lost its monopoly cellular telephone market two years ago, but competition in overseas calling poses much bigger problems for the company.
The Israeli international calling market has grown rapidly in recent years and accounted for 25.5 percent of Bezeq's revenues in 1996.
Although Bezeq has cut its international tariffs in recent years, analysts say they account for far more than a quarter of the company's profits and have traditionally subsidised the local service.

"It is difficult to get information on the international calling segment because Bezeq stopped releasing it in anticipation of competition," said Dany Koninsky of Bank Hapoalim. "I assume (profitability) is very high."
Analysts say it is premature to try estimating the damage to Bezeq from competition in international calling.

The government's rules for the new, competitive market make it easy for customers to choose between Bezeq and its two competitors -- Barak and Golden Lines, which are each controlled by consortiums of foreign and local companies.
To meet the competition Bezeq has been allowed to cut its tariffs, but Golden Lines' and Barak's rates are generally lower.
Levitan notes, however, that Bezeq's Pelephone cellular telephone subsidiary held up well when it began facing competition from Cellcom in 1995.
"No one guessed that price sensitivity was so low in the cellular telephone market that people were willing to sign up with Pelephone even though Cellcom's tariffs were much lower," said Levitan.
Bezeq will also benefit from interconnection fees to the two new international providers, especially if Israelis begin making many more overseas calls.

Bezeq, for instance, is getting 0.52 shekel ($0.15) a minute for each call to North America that goes through its network to Barak, Golden Lines or Bezeq's own international-calling subsidiary, Bezeq International. The rate falls to 0.40 shekel in 1998.
Since Barak and Golden Lines are charging 0.65 shekel a minute or less, most of their revenues will flow back to Bezeq.
But even if it takes the lion's share of revenues, Levitan said, Bezeq's profits on each call will be lower than if the call were placed through it exclusively at the old rates.

Other factors will play a role in Bezeq's earnings outlook, analysts note. The government is cutting the level of royalties Bezeq pays it and Pelephone is a growing profit centre. On the other hand, Bezeq will be taking write-offs for redundancies.
Koninsky is bearish on future profits, seeing Bezeq's earnings per share (EPS) falling to 0.73 shekel this year and to 0.70 shekel in 1998.

Levitan estimates EPS will drop to 0.72 shekel this year but rise to 0.75 shekel in 1998, compared with 0.92 shekel in 1996. "It will be a difficult transition but inside one or two years it will return to its old level of profitability," said Levitan.

Saddled with the uncertainty surrounding competition, Bezeq shares are trading at about 14 times Hapoalim's 1997 prospective earnings estimate. Bezeq closed at 10.26 shekels on Monday on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
Levitan said on an international comparison that makes Bezeq shares cheap. Telecoms companies elsewhere in the world, he added, "are in the same competitive mud."
